title: Research weaving to mobilise expert‐curated knowledge for species conservation: Case study of the diamond‐backed terrapin—A protocol
content:
Species- and system-level working groups accumulate decades of expert knowledge but rarely formalise their role as evidence synthesisers. Integrated evidence synthesis and bibliometric approaches offer a systematic framework for transforming these groups into formal curators of system-specific scientific knowledge. Using the diamond-backed terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin) as a case study, we demonstrate a scalable, reproducible workflow applicable to any taxon or system with an associated scientific literature.


Abstract

Conservation biology increasingly relies on peer-reviewed evidence to derive model parameters, inform management strategies and guide policy, yet incomplete literature coverage and publication bias can compromise the quality of that evidence base. Species- and system-level working groups represent collaborative networks of experts uniquely positioned to address these gaps, but formal and systematic synthesis and dissemination of their own accumulated literature bases has rarely been part of their mandate. Here we demonstrate the practical benefits of working group-driven systematic literature curation and dissemination through research weaving, a literature synthesis framework integrating systematic mapping and bibliometric analysis. As a case study for this framework, we partner with the Diamondback Terrapin Working Group (DTWG), a consortium of scientists dedicated to the ecology and conservation of the diamond-backed terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin), a threatened turtle endemic to the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States and Bermuda. Specifically, we aim to (1) characterise spatial, temporal and conceptual knowledge gaps and knowledge clusters within the M. terrapin literature; (2) appraise the M. terrapin literature's use of open and transparent research practices, including data and code sharing, ethics approval and funding disclosure; and (3) identify co-authorship networks to examine how geographic and institutional associations shape M. terrapin knowledge production and policy-document citation rates. We will screen the expert-curated DTWG bibliography and records from six bibliographic databases against pre-defined population–concept–context eligibility criteria, using independent reviewers at title/abstract and full-text stages. Data will be extracted using a human-validated, large language model-assisted workflow. We will synthesise the evidence base using evidence heatmaps and co-occurrence plots, examine temporal trends in transparency reporting and analyse co-authorship networks and scientific and policy-document citation rates. Practical implication: Research weaving offers a rigorous framework for species- or system-level experts to document the conceptual scope, collaborative structure and real-world policy impact of their empirical evidence bases. This study will provide a scalable, AI-integrated and reproducible workflow for working-group-mediated research weaving, offering a practical model for transforming expert communities into formal curators of system-specific scientific knowledge.
